spans.text: Boundedness
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A real sequence is an ordered list a₁, a₂, a₃, … indexed by the positive integers. Its order and
repetitions matter. The set of values taken by a sequence does not retain all this information.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A sequence is bounded above if there is a real number U such that aₙ ≤ U for every n. It is
bounded below if there is a real number L such that L ≤ aₙ for every n. It is bounded if both
conditions hold. Equivalently, there is M ≥ 0 with |aₙ| ≤ M for every n.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
The sequence aₙ = 1/n is bounded: 0 < aₙ ≤ 1 for every positive integer n. The sequence bₙ =
(−1)ⁿ is also bounded, because −1 ≤ bₙ ≤ 1. Boundedness describes where the terms can lie; it
does not say that they approach a single value.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A bound need not be a term of the sequence, and it need not be the best possible bound. For aₙ
= 1/n, both 1 and 2 are upper bounds, but 1 is the least upper bound of the set of values. The
lower bound 0 is never attained.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Do not confuse “all terms remain in a fixed finite interval” with “the terms eventually stay close
to one point.” The first describes boundedness; the second belongs to convergence.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Questions to explain
What does a bound have to control? Can a bounded sequence keep oscillating? Must a lower bound
be one of the terms?
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text: Convergence and quantifiers
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A sequence aₙ converges to a real number ℓ if, for every ε > 0, there exists a positive integer N
such that, for every n ≥ N, |aₙ − ℓ| < ε.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
The order of the choices matters. N may depend on ε, but after N has been selected it must
work for every later index n. The definition does not allow a new N to be chosen separately for
each term.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
For aₙ = 1/n, given ε > 0, choose an integer N > 1/ε. For every n ≥ N, 0 < 1/n ≤ 1/N < ε. Thus
the sequence converges to 0.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Every convergent real sequence is bounded. To see this, use ε = 1 to place all sufficiently late
terms in the interval (ℓ − 1, ℓ + 1). There are only finitely many earlier terms. A sufficiently large
bound can cover those terms as well as the tail.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
The converse is false. The bounded sequence bₙ = (−1)ⁿ alternates between −1 and 1 and does
not converge. If it converged to ℓ, then for ε = 1/2 all sufficiently late terms would lie within 1/2
of ℓ. Taking a late even index and a late odd index would give 2 = |1 − (−1)| ≤ |1 − ℓ| + |ℓ + 1|
< 1, a contradiction.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Questions to explain
Why must the same N work for all later terms? Why do finitely many early terms not prevent
convergence or boundedness? Why is boundedness insufficient for convergence?
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text: Monotone convergence
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A sequence is nondecreasing if aₙ₊₁ ≥ aₙ for every n. It is nonincreasing if aₙ₊₁ ≤ aₙ for every n. A
sequence is monotone if it has either of these properties. Equal consecutive terms are allowed.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text: Every bounded monotone sequence of real numbers converges.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
More precisely, a nondecreasing sequence that is bounded above converges to the supremum
of its set of values. A nonincreasing sequence that is bounded below converges to the infimum
of its set of values.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Proof in the nondecreasing case: Let s be the supremum of {aₙ : n ≥ 1}, which exists by
completeness. Given ε > 0, s − ε cannot be an upper bound for all the terms. Therefore some
term a_N satisfies s − ε < a_N ≤ s. By monotonicity, for every n ≥ N we have s − ε < a_N ≤ aₙ ≤
s. Hence |aₙ − s| < ε, proving convergence to s.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Both ideas matter. Boundedness supplies a finite supremum; monotonicity makes the entire tail
stay above the term already found near that supremum. Boundedness alone permits oscillation.
Monotonicity alone permits divergence to infinity, as with aₙ = n.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Questions to explain
Where is completeness used? Where is monotonicity used? Why does finding just one term near s
not by itself control every later term?
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text: Subsequences
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A subsequence of aₙ is a sequence aₙₖ obtained by choosing a strictly increasing sequence of
positive integer indices n₁ < n₂ < n₃ < …. The indices must keep moving forward, but the values
need not be increasing.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
If aₙ converges to ℓ, every subsequence also converges to ℓ. Given ε > 0, choose N for the
original sequence. Strictly increasing positive integer indices satisfy nₖ ≥ k. Therefore, when k ≥
N, the term aₙₖ is also far enough along the original sequence to be within ε of ℓ.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
A convergent subsequence does not imply that the whole sequence converges. For bₙ = (−1)ⁿ,
the even-indexed subsequence is constantly 1 and the odd-indexed subsequence is constantly
−1. Each subsequence converges, but the original sequence does not.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
The Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem for real sequences states that every bounded real sequence
has a convergent subsequence. It guarantees a convergent subsequence, not convergence of
the entire sequence.
spans.quality: native-text; line-level location; formulas may need visual checking

spans.text:
Questions to explain
Why must subsequence indices be strictly increasing? How do the even and odd subsequences
distinguish boundedness from convergence? Which word changes the claim in Bolzano–Weierstrass?
